The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing radially outside the annular guide 18 so that no part of the mounting boss 70 reaches into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the annular frame body and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending outward from it, away from the frame. The latch 16 is drawn in its over-center position, in which the pipe 90 is clamped; the lever attitude there is shown schematically.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, one at the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each crosses the inner boundary of that body and reaches radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost lies on the first frame half 10 and the other two on the second frame half 12; those positions and their apportionment between the halves are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined to it at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the outer surface of the pipe 90, its depth shown schematically.

A broken cutting-plane line runs along the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, extending past the outer boundary of the annular frame body at one end and past the jaw pad 40 at the other, with a short arrow at each end pointing to the same side, the viewing direction of FIG. 3.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer boundary of the annular frame body at its upper right.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body at its right.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the block of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the topmost carriage inner end.
- 90 pipe: target well inside the central circle.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring from the same side as FIG. 1 is viewed, so that the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, no shading, well inside the drawing area. The form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints is shown schematically.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area, bounded by inner and outer circular boundaries, is the segmented cam ring 20. The space inside is empty.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings pass through the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, spaced from one another and from both joints; those circumferential positions, and the passage of each opening through the annulus, are shown schematically. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the width of the annulus and inclined to the radius at its own position, so that one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. In each slot the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary; that handedness, and the corresponding sense of ring rotation, are shown schematically.

Near the right joint, the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24 runs as a short straight surface slanting inward toward that joint, the ring drive face 36. Which segment carries it, and its position on the outer boundary, are shown schematically.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary of the annulus in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment, in its upper left.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment, at the bottom.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface near the right joint.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer removed over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments inside the frame are visible. Radially outward is toward the right of the view and the circumferential direction runs from top to bottom. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. No structure lying outside the frame at this joint is shown. Shown schematically: the extent of the region shown, the proportions of the bodies, and the form of the meeting surfaces at the joint.

Two bodies occupy the upper and lower parts of the view. Each is bounded on the left by an arc and on the right by an arc concentric with it, and each ends toward the middle of the view at a straight end face that runs from the left boundary to the right boundary. The two end faces face one another across a narrow gap. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Within the upper body lies a hatched block that follows the two arcuate boundaries, is spaced inward from each of them, and reaches down to the end face of that body. That block is the first cam ring segment 22.

Within the lower body lies a like hatched block, spaced inward from both arcuate boundaries of that body and reaching up to its end face. That block is the second cam ring segment 24.

The lower end of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end of the second cam ring segment 24 meet in the gap along complementary surfaces that face one another and are in contact, so that the two blocks read as one arcuate body interrupted at the joint. Those meeting surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

The two bodies of the frame are drawn in outline and the two cam ring segments carry hatching, so that each segment reads as a separate body held within its own frame half.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the hatching of the upper block.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the hatching of the lower block.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces in the gap.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the annular frame body and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending outward from it, away from the frame. The latch 16 is drawn in its over-center position, in which the pipe 90 is clamped; the lever attitude there is shown schematically.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, one at the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each crosses the inner boundary of that body and reaches radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost lies on the first frame half 10 and the other two on the second frame half 12; those positions and their apportionment between the halves are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined to it at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the outer surface of the pipe 90, its depth shown schematically.

A broken cutting-plane line runs along the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, extending past the outer boundary of the annular frame body at one end and past the jaw pad 40 at the other, with a short arrow at each end pointing to the same side. That line is the cutting plane of the sectional view of FIG. 3, and the two arrows give the direction in which that section is viewed.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer boundary of the annular frame body at its upper right.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body at its right.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the block of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the topmost carriage inner end.
- 90 pipe: target well inside the central circle.

input.summary: Fixed all four findings. The section-line mismatch is resolved by making the specification and the FIG. 1 brief describe the same thing: the Brief Description and the detailed description now say FIG. 3 is taken on the plane indicated by the cutting-plane line and arrows in FIG. 1, and the FIG. 1 brief states that the line it specifies is the cutting plane of the FIG. 3 section with the arrows giving the viewing direction, so the specification no longer refers to a designation that the sheet does not carry. Numeral 16 is removed from the FIG. 4 numeral list, leaving one numeral per body on that sheet and keeping 16 on the latch as a whole in FIG. 1. FIG. 2 now marks the passage of each slot opening through the annulus as shown schematically, matching the hedge already in FIG. 3. Claims 4 and 12 now recite that the coupled ring has been rotated by the wedge so as to advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism, removing the implication that the full stroke is completed at the over-center position. I also removed two generic negative rendering controls from the figure briefs while preserving the geometry they were guarding.
reasoning: Section-line finding: the defect is a mismatch between text that names a designation and a brief that specifies no such designation, and it can be closed from either side. I closed it from the text side because the image pipeline renders unlabeled geometry and then adds only the listed reference numerals, the FIG. label, callouts and leaders. A numeral 3 placed at the arrowheads would be drawing text the geometry stage cannot produce, and if it did appear it would be a numeral on the sheet with no entry in numerals.md, which is itself a defect. Referring instead to the plane indicated by the cutting-plane line and arrows in FIG. 1 makes both places point at geometry the FIG. 1 brief actually specifies, and I strengthened that brief so the line is expressly identified as the cutting plane of the FIG. 3 section rather than merely carrying arrows in the FIG. 3 viewing direction. The sectional relationship, the plane through the carriage radial direction and the frame axis, and the arrows showing the viewing direction are all preserved.

Numeral 16 on FIG. 4: the only enclosure on that sheet is the latch housing 58, so a second leader from 16 to the same body invited the reading that 16 names a distinct part. Deleting the list entry was the whole fix, because every latch component visible on the sheet already has its own numeral (50, 52, 54, 56, 58) and 16 is placed on the latch as a whole in FIG. 1. No numeral definition, part, or specification text was deleted: the detailed description still says the latch 16 includes the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52 and the force-limiting spring stack 54, which is what relates 16 to those parts.

FIG. 2 slot topology: the disclosure says only that each carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot, so whether the slot is a through-opening or a blind groove is a depiction choice, not a disclosed fact. FIG. 3 already hedged it and FIG. 2 did not. I added the passage of each opening through the annulus to FIG. 2's schematic hedge so both sheets treat it as a convention. The description and claims needed no change, since they say only that the follower is received in the oblique slot, and I did not import the through-opening into the text.

Claims 4 and 12: claim 1 defines the stroke as the rotation that advances the carriages inwardly, and the description teaches that the pads land partway through at a point set by the pipe diameter, with the remaining handle travel going into the spring stack instead of turning the ring farther. Reciting that the ring has been rotated through the stroke at the over-center position contradicted that teaching and bought no scope. The replacement wording, rotated by the wedge so as to advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism, keeps the disclosed over-center function, uses only terms with antecedent basis in claims 1 and 10, and matches the description word for word. Claim 1 and the method claims were untouched, so the fallback ladder is unchanged.

While in the briefs I removed two generic negative rendering controls that the current instructions call out. FIG. 2's no shading was a style ban unrelated to invention geometry and is gone; the other briefs never had it. FIG. 6's blanket statement that no structure outside the frame is shown is replaced by a positive statement of what the fragmentary view contains, namely the two frame ends meeting at the joint and the cam ring segment ends held within them. FIG. 5's statement that no part of the mounting boss reaches into the groove was kept, because that is the inventor's own relationship, that the boss lies outside the annular guide and does not participate in jaw synchronization, and not a rendering control.

I checked the endpoint targets against the current rules while making these edits and left them alone: they use broad interior targets such as well inside the block or the hatching, they distinguish parts by explicit position words such as topmost, upper, lower, left and right rather than by direction-ambiguous ordinals, and the few surface targets, such as the groove wall above the block and the right wall of the channel below the groove mouth, are there to separate the guide from the body running in it rather than to fix an aesthetic coordinate.

Nothing was added to the claims, description, numeral table or disclosed embodiments to accommodate anything drawn. All 26 numerals still appear in the description and in the table exactly once each, every numeral used in a brief is in the table, and sheet loads are now 8, 7, 8, 7, 4 and 5.
changes: draft/07-drawings.md: FIG. 3 entry now reads taken on the plane indicated by the cutting-plane line and arrows in FIG. 1, in place of taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1.
draft/08-detailed-description.md: the FIG. 3 paragraph makes the same change, so no passage refers to a 3-3 designation.

figures/FIG-1.md: the cutting-plane paragraph now identifies that line as the cutting plane of the sectional view of FIG. 3 and states that the two arrows give the direction in which that section is viewed.
figures/FIG-4.md: deleted the numeral list entry placing 16 on the outer surface of the enclosure's left wall; the sheet now lists 20, 36, 50, 52, 54, 56 and 58.
figures/FIG-2.md: the slot paragraph now marks the circumferential positions and the passage of each opening through the annulus as shown schematically, matching the hedge in FIG. 3.

draft/09-claims.md: in claims 4 and 12, replaced and the coupled ring has been rotated through the stroke with and the coupled ring has been rotated by the wedge so as to advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism.
figures/FIG-2.md: removed the no shading rendering control from the header.

figures/FIG-6.md: replaced the blanket exclusion of structure outside the frame with a positive statement that the view is confined to the two frame ends meeting at the joint and the cam ring segment ends held within them.
input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the Background cites none, so there was again nothing to read, cite or design around, and the art available to this draft remains incomplete because no search was run. None of this turn's edits touched the feature the independent claims rest on: a cam ring that is split with the clamp body, one segment travelling with each frame half, whose complementary coupling faces at both the hinge end and the latch end are brought into engagement by the act of closing the frame, so that a single latch input reaches all three carriages through oblique slots as one coupled ring. The claim 4 and 12 amendment narrows nothing of that combination; it only removes an internal inconsistency about when ring rotation ends, and the Background's account of the two problems the combination solves, off-centre settling from independently driven half-drives and concentrated jaw loading from a rigid drive train, is unchanged and still available for any later argument.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer removed over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments inside the frame are visible. Radially outward is toward the right of the view and the circumferential direction runs from top to bottom. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. The view is confined to the two frame ends that meet at this joint and to the cam ring segment ends held within them. Shown schematically: the extent of the region shown, the proportions of the bodies, and the form of the meeting surfaces at the joint.

Two bodies occupy the upper and lower parts of the view. Each is bounded on the left by an arc and on the right by an arc concentric with it, and each ends toward the middle of the view at a straight end face that runs from the left boundary to the right boundary. The two end faces face one another across a narrow gap. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Within the upper body lies a hatched block that follows the two arcuate boundaries, is spaced inward from each of them, and reaches down to the end face of that body. That block is the first cam ring segment 22.

Within the lower body lies a like hatched block, spaced inward from both arcuate boundaries of that body and reaching up to its end face. That block is the second cam ring segment 24.

The lower end of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end of the second cam ring segment 24 meet in the gap along complementary surfaces that face one another and are in contact, so that the two blocks read as one arcuate body interrupted at the joint. Those meeting surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

The two bodies of the frame are drawn in outline and the two cam ring segments carry hatching, so that each segment reads as a separate body held within its own frame half.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the hatching of the upper block.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the hatching of the lower block.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces in the gap.

FIG. 5 is an enlarged fragmentary sectional view taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3, through a frame provided with the optional mounting boss, and showing equipment supported on the mounting boss.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments inside the frame are visible. Radially outward is toward the right of the view and the circumferential direction runs from top to bottom. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and to the ends of the two cam ring segments carried there. Shown schematically: the extent of the region shown, the proportions of the bodies, and the form of the meeting surfaces at the joint.

Two bodies occupy the upper and lower parts of the view. Each is bounded on the left by an arc and on the right by an arc concentric with it, and each ends toward the middle of the view at a straight end face that runs from the left boundary to the right boundary. The two end faces face one another across a narrow gap. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Within the upper body lies a block drawn in outline that follows the two arcuate boundaries, is spaced inward from each of them, and reaches down past the end face of that body into the gap. That block is the first cam ring segment 22.

Within the lower body lies a like block drawn in outline, spaced inward from both arcuate boundaries of that body and reaching up past its end face into the gap. That block is the second cam ring segment 24.

The lower end of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end of the second cam ring segment 24 meet in the gap along complementary surfaces that face one another and are in contact, so that the two blocks read as one arcuate body interrupted at the joint. Those meeting surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

The two bodies of the frame are broken away at the near wall and carry section hatching, and the two cam ring segments are drawn in outline within them, so that each segment reads as a separate body held within its own frame half.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target the hatching of the upper body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatching of the lower body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper block.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower block.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces in the gap.

content.text: Both FIG. 6 findings are fixed, with the drawing description and endpoints brought into step.

input.summary: Repaired both FIG. 6 defects. The cam ring segment ends now reach past their own frame end faces into the gap, so the contact the brief requires at the coupling faces is drawable and the sheet cannot be executed with the two segments separated. The broken-away view now follows the normal convention: the frame is broken away at the near wall and carries section hatching, the cam ring segments revealed behind it are drawn in outline, and the opening paragraph announces the hatching rule the rest of the set uses. The FIG. 6 entry in the Brief Description of the Drawings now says the near wall is broken away and the frame is shown in section at the break, and the two frame-half endpoints on that sheet now target hatching while the two segment endpoints target the outlined blocks. No claim, numeral, or disclosed relationship changed.
reasoning: The contact finding went to the one sheet whose purpose is to show the disclosed coupling, so the fix had to make contact drawable rather than soften the language. Each segment now reaches down or up past its own frame end face into the gap, which lets the two ends meet along complementary surfaces in contact exactly as the following paragraph requires. I left the contact sentence untouched, because it states the inventor's essential relationship that closure couples the segments so they move as one ring, and that sentence is what the description leans on when it says the two ends meet at the complementary coupling faces 28. FIG. 4 already depicts the same joint the same way, with a narrow radial gap and the band ends meeting in it, so the set is now consistent across both views of that joint.

The hatching finding was a convention inversion, not a geometry question. In a broken-away view the material cut by the break is the frame wall, and what lies behind it is seen in elevation, so I swapped the two: the frame bodies now carry section hatching and the segment blocks are drawn in outline. The reason the hatching was there in the first place, that each segment must read as a separate body carried by its own frame half, survives the swap because the outlined segment blocks now interrupt the frame hatching. I also added the same opening clause the other sectional briefs carry, that cut solid material carries section hatching, so FIG. 6 announces the rule the rest of the set announces.

Because the hatching moved, the leader endpoints had to move with it or they would point at surfaces that no longer exist. Numerals 10 and 12 now target the hatching of their frame body, clear of the block lying in it, which is the broad interior target that distinguishes the frame half from the segment inside it. Numerals 22 and 24 now target well inside their block rather than inside hatching that the blocks no longer carry. No exact depth, midpoint or quarter modifier was introduced, and the sheet uses upper and lower rather than ordinals whose direction could be read either way.

Two consequential edits were needed to keep the files synchronized. The Brief Description's FIG. 6 entry now says the near wall is broken away and the frame is shown in section at the break, matching the brief. Inside the brief I also adjusted two phrases that would have become internally inconsistent once the segments project into the gap: the view is now described as confined to the two frame ends at the joint and the ends of the two cam ring segments carried there, and the closing sentence says each segment reads as a separate body carried by its own frame half rather than held within it.

Nothing in the claims, the detailed description, the numeral table or the disclosed embodiments was touched. The description's FIG. 6 sentence already recites the contacting reading, so it needed no change, and the numeral table is unchanged with FIG. 6 still carrying 10, 12, 22, 24 and 28.

This turn touched only FIG. 6 and its Brief Description entry, so the feature the independent claims rest on is unchanged: a cam ring split with the clamp body, one segment travelling with each frame half, whose complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and the latch end are brought into engagement by the act of closing the frame so that a single latch input reaches all three carriages through oblique slots as one coupled ring. The FIG. 6 repair in fact strengthens the depiction of that feature, since the sheet can no longer be rendered with the two segment ends apart, which would have shown the coupled ring uncoupled.

Two neighbouring phrases in the brief were adjusted so nothing contradicts the segments now projecting into the gap. The claims, detailed description, numeral table and every other figure file are unchanged and remain in step, with FIG. 6 still carrying numerals 10, 12, 22, 24 and 28.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments inside the frame are visible. Radially outward is toward the right of the view and the circumferential direction runs from top to bottom. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and to the ends of the two cam ring segments carried there. Shown schematically: the extent of the region shown, the proportions of the bodies, and the form of the meeting surfaces at the joint.

Two bodies occupy the upper and lower parts of the view. Each is bounded on the left by an arc and on the right by an arc concentric with it, and each ends toward the middle of the view at a straight end face that runs from the left boundary to the right boundary. The two end faces face one another across a narrow gap. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Within the upper body lies a block drawn in outline that follows the two arcuate boundaries, is spaced inward from each of them, and reaches down past the end face of that body into the gap. That block is the first cam ring segment 22.

Within the lower body lies a like block drawn in outline, spaced inward from both arcuate boundaries of that body and reaching up past its end face into the gap. That block is the second cam ring segment 24.

The lower end of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end of the second cam ring segment 24 meet in the gap along complementary surfaces that face one another and are in contact, so that the two blocks read as one arcuate body interrupted at the joint. Those meeting surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

The two bodies of the frame are broken away at the near wall and carry section hatching, and the two cam ring segments are drawn in outline, so that each segment reads as a separate body carried by its own frame half.

- 10 first frame half: target the hatching of the upper body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatching of the lower body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper block.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower block.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces in the gap.

input.summary: Extended the schematic hedges in the two latch-end figure briefs so the drafted joint geometry is expressly a depiction convention. FIG. 6 now hedges the narrow gap between the two frame end faces and the extent to which each cam ring segment end projects into that gap, alongside the hedges it already carried. FIG. 4 now hedges the narrow gap between the two frame ends and the projection of the band ends into it. No file in draft/ was touched: the claims, detailed description, Brief Description of the Drawings, numeral table and abstract are unchanged, and the geometry both sheets must show, namely the two segment ends meeting in contact at the coupling faces, is unchanged.
reasoning: The finding is that the latch-end joint geometry, frame ends spaced apart with each segment end projecting into the gap, is a contact-and-location relationship the inventor never stated, and it was the only such choice in the set without a schematic hedge. Since the application text is already neutral about it, the cure belongs entirely in the briefs, so I added the hedge there and changed nothing in draft/. Putting the gap into the description or claims would have imported a drafted depiction choice into the invention, which is exactly the wrong direction.

In FIG. 6 the hedge list previously covered the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies and the form of the meeting surfaces, that is how the surfaces are shaped rather than whether the frame ends are separated. It now also covers the narrow gap between the two frame end faces and how far each segment end projects into it. FIG. 4's list covered the joint surfaces but not the gap, and now covers the narrow gap between the two frame ends and the projection of the band ends into it.

I kept the contact sentences in both briefs exactly as they were. The gap and the projection distance are depiction choices and are now hedged, but the fact that the two segment ends meet in contact at the coupling faces is the inventor's own essential relationship, that closure couples the segments so they move as one ring, and it must remain an unhedged requirement or FIG. 6 could again be rendered showing the coupled ring uncoupled, which was the major finding repaired last turn.

Both edited briefs remain within the length limit, FIG. 4 at 2703 characters and FIG. 6 at 2775, and no numeral, endpoint or geometric relationship moved, so the numeral table, the drawing descriptions and the four untouched briefs stay in step.

Hedging the gap in fact keeps that feature clean, because the coupling now reads as a disclosed relationship rather than as the particular joint layout the sheets happen to draw.
